content: Interpreting test results and reporting HIV status should be conducted with precision and care, followed by offering post-test counseling to address the emotional and psychological needs of the individual. It is essential to ensure that individuals are linked to appropriate prevention, treatment, and care services to manage their health effectively. Peer workers can be trained to act as lay providers, enabling them to perform these tasks under supervision. In a triage testing approach, a trained provider administers a single rapid diagnostic test (RDT) and facilitates linkage to further confirmatory testing and services based on the initial result. For individuals with a reactive HIV test result, prompt referral to confirmatory testing is critical to establish their HIV status. This strategy is also applicable in self-testing initiatives and can be expanded to community-based testing programs led by lay providers. Integration of HIV testing with other health services involves the co-delivery and sharing of resources across various health domains. This includes not only providing related health services in a common facility or community setting but also connecting patient records and reporting systems to share information securely, with the client’s consent. This integration ensures appropriate referrals between services and providers. For HIV, this may involve person-centered delivery of testing, prevention, treatment, and care services alongside other health services in community or facility settings. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends integrating HIV services, including HIV testing services (HTS), in all epidemic settings, particularly in high-burden areas. HTS can be offered at public and private health facilities and other service points identified as key entry points, such as sexually transmitted infection (STI) clinics, tuberculosis (TB) clinics, antenatal care (ANC) services, family planning programs, and community-based programs targeting key populations. The primary goal of integration is to increase coverage and impact by diagnosing more people for HIV and other diseases simultaneously, which is both cost-effective and resource-saving. Lay providers, when adequately trained and supervised, can independently conduct safe and effective HIV testing using RDTs. This task-sharing approach is strongly recommended by WHO, supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Facility-based HTS involves routinely offering testing within various health facilities, which is a cornerstone of the HIV response. Standalone voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) sites, often linked to health facilities, remain a valuable option for reaching populations less likely to access traditional clinical services, such as men and key populations. Self-testing within facilities can save healthcare worker time and increase testing capacity, particularly in settings with suboptimal coverage. ANC services should routinely offer HTS to all pregnant women, along with testing for syphilis and hepatitis B, as early as possible during pregnancy to achieve the triple elimination of mother-to-child transmission. Dual HIV/syphilis RDTs are recommended as the first test in ANC settings and for key populations. Family planning services provide an opportunity to integrate HTS as part of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and HIV prevention packages, particularly in high HIV burden settings where women seeking contraception may have a high incidence of HIV. Pediatric services in high HIV burden settings should offer HTS to infants and children with unknown HIV status who are admitted for inpatient care or attending outpatient, malnutrition, or immunization clinics. Testing should also be offered to parents with unknown HIV status. Testing HIV-exposed or hospitalized children and those with a biological parent living with HIV remains a critical strategy for identifying additional children living with HIV. TB services should routinely offer HTS to all clients with presumptive or confirmed TB in any setting. Intensified TB case finding among people with HIV is essential to facilitate early detection and treatment, as TB is a leading cause of death among people with HIV. Specialized facility-based services for key populations, such as drop-in centers and harm reduction services for people who inject drugs, can improve access to HTS. These services are particularly important in settings where key populations face barriers to accessing health facilities. Community-based HTS refers to services offered outside of health facilities, such as outreach to hotspots, workplaces, and educational establishments. WHO recommends community-based HTS to increase uptake among key populations, young people, men, and others less likely to visit facilities. Community-led HTS is an important component of differentiated service delivery (DSD) and can include mobile vans, home-based testing, and self-testing. Workplace HTS is an effective strategy for reaching men in high-burden settings and can be implemented within workplace policies that ensure confidentiality and protect workers from discrimination. Mobile outreach can complement facility-based HTS in areas with low coverage and poor accessibility, reaching highly mobile populations. Faith-based HTS, including self-testing, can be a promising approach for reaching undiagnosed individuals. Home-based HTS has the potential to reach undiagnosed people in high-burden settings and can effectively target men if offered outside of work hours. It is also useful for network-based testing to reach children of people with HIV. Community campaigns, including self-testing, may be useful when offered periodically in high HIV burden settings. However, in low-burden settings, campaigns should focus on priority populations with high ongoing risk. School-based HTS can serve as an entry point for adolescents, particularly in high HIV incidence settings, and can be integrated with broader HIV prevention and SRH services. Network-based testing approaches involve supporting individuals to disclose, refer for testing, or distribute self-tests to partners, families, and social networks. These strategies may include testing for sexual and injecting partners, family members, and social contacts. Integration of network-based testing services across conditions should be considered based on local epidemiology and available resources. Provider-assisted partner services should be offered to all people with HIV as part of a voluntary comprehensive package of testing, care, and prevention. HIV testing services for couples and partners, with support for mutual disclosure, should be offered to individuals with known HIV status and their partners. STI partner services should also be offered as part of a comprehensive package of voluntary STI testing, care, and prevention. All partner services must be voluntary, protect privacy, and ensure confidentiality.
